Write \(E_0=E_{P_{0,O}}\). We first profile the PT restriction. By \(\mathrm{def{:}restriction\text{-}maps}\),
\[
 q_{\mathrm{PT},x}=\delta_1^0(x)\mathbf 1_J-D(x),
 \qquad A_{\mathrm{PT}}=I_J-J^{-1}\mathbf 1_J\mathbf 1_J^{\prime}.
 \tag{1}
\]
Since \(\mathbf 1_J^{\prime}\mathbf 1_J=J\),
\[
 A_{\mathrm{PT}}\mathbf 1_J=0,
 \qquad
 A_{\mathrm{PT}}\dot q_{\mathrm{PT},x}=-A_{\mathrm{PT}}\dot D(x).
 \tag{2}
\]
Thus profiling the unrestricted scalar path \(\dot\delta_1^0(x)\) leaves precisely the observed derivative of \(-A_{\mathrm{PT}}D(x)\). The matrix \(A_{\mathrm{PT}}\) is the orthogonal projector onto \(\{v:\mathbf 1_J^{\prime}v=0\}\), so it has rank \(J-1\). If \(\widetilde R_{D,x}\) represents \(\dot D(x)\), then \(R_{\mathrm{PT},x}=-A_{\mathrm{PT}}\widetilde R_{D,x}\), and hence
\[
 \operatorname{rank}E_0[R_{\mathrm{PT},x}R_{\mathrm{PT},x}^{\prime}]
 \le J-1.
 \tag{3}
\]
Equality holds when the covariance form is positive definite on the range of \(A_{\mathrm{PT}}\), exactly as stated.

For SC put \(\Pi_x=B(x)\{B(x)^{\prime}B(x)\}^{-1}B(x)^{\prime}\). Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}sc\text{-}rank}\) gives an invertible Gram matrix, so \(\Pi_x\) is the orthogonal projector onto the \(J\)-dimensional column space of \(B(x)\). At an SC law \(a(x)=B(x)w(x)\). Differentiating \(\Pi_xB(x)=B(x)\) and then \(r_{\mathrm{SC},x}=(I_T-\Pi_x)a(x)\) gives
\[
 \dot r_{\mathrm{SC},x}
 =(I_T-\Pi_x)\{\dot a(x)-\dot B(x)w(x)\}.
 \tag{4}
\]
Therefore the covariance range of \(R_{\mathrm{SC},x}\) lies in \(\operatorname{range}(I_T-\Pi_x)\), whose dimension is \(T-J\). This proves the SC rank ceiling, and positive definiteness of the residualized covariance form on that range gives equality.

The conditional-residual normalizations used above are available without a new hypothesis. For every occupied cell, quotient differentiation gives
\[
 \dot\mu_{g,t}(x;s)
 =E_0\!\left[
 \frac{\mathbf 1\{G=g,X=x\}}{p_X(x)p_g(x)}
 \{Y_t-\mu_{g,t}(x)\}s\right].
 \tag{5}
\]
The bracketed residual has conditional mean zero given \((G,X)\). Both \(r_{b,x}\) and \(C_b(x)\) are differentiable finite-dimensional functions of these cell means under the displayed rank condition. Applying the ordinary chain rule to (5) therefore constructs versions of \(R_{b,x}\) and \(g^{\circ}_{b,x}\) as linear combinations of such residuals, proving their defining covariance equations and conditional centering.

We next obtain the tangent spaces. The PT observed projection is locally the zero set of \(r_{\mathrm{PT},x}=-A_{\mathrm{PT}}D(x)\): the equality \(A_{\mathrm{PT}}D(x)=0\) is equivalent to \(D(x)=c(x)\mathbf 1_J\), and one can choose the missing treated untreated final mean as \(\mu_{1,T-1}(x)+c(x)\). The SC observed projection is locally the zero set of \(r_{\mathrm{SC},x}=(I_T-\Pi_x)a(x)\): full column rank gives
\[
 r_{\mathrm{SC},x}=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a(x)=B(x)w(x),
 \tag{6}
\]
and the missing treated untreated final mean can be chosen as \(w(x)^{\prime}\mu_{C,T}(x)\). These choices preserve the observed law and impose the corresponding full-data restriction. No anticipation justifies using observed preperiod and donor means in both constructions; overlap makes every conditional mean well defined.

Differentiating the branch equations along a branch-preserving path gives
\[
 E_0[R_{b,x}s]=0\quad\text{for every }x.
 \tag{7}
\]
Conversely, retain a maximal linearly independent coordinate vector \(R_b^{*}\). Constant rank permits the same coordinate choice locally. Its Gram matrix is positive definite. Truncating and recentering its coordinates produces a bounded vector \(v\) for which \(M=E_0[R_b^{*}v^{\prime}]\) is nonsingular. For a bounded, mean-zero score \(s\) satisfying (7), use the exponential tilt
\[
 \frac{dP_{O,\varepsilon,c}}{dP_{0,O}}
 =\frac{\exp\{\varepsilon s+c^{\prime}v\}}
 {E_0[\exp\{\varepsilon s+c^{\prime}v\}]},
 \qquad F(\varepsilon,c)=r_b^{*}(P_{O,\varepsilon,c}).
 \tag{8}
\]
Finite support, overlap, bounded tilting directions, and the fourth-moment condition justify differentiation of the conditional means. At the origin,
\[
 F(0,0)=0,
 \qquad \partial_cF(0,0)=M,
 \qquad \partial_{\varepsilon}F(0,0)=E_0[R_b^{*}s]=0.
 \tag{9}
\]
We derive the correction directly. Differentiability and (9) give
\[
 F(\varepsilon,c)=F(\varepsilon,0)+Mc+\zeta(\varepsilon,c),
 \qquad F(\varepsilon,0)=o(\varepsilon),
\]
where, on a sufficiently small ball, the Lipschitz constant of \(c\mapsto M^{-1}\zeta(\varepsilon,c)\) is at most \(1/2\). Hence
\[
 \mathcal K_\varepsilon(c)=-M^{-1}\{F(\varepsilon,0)+\zeta(\varepsilon,c)\}
\]
maps a ball of radius \(C|\varepsilon|\) into itself and is a contraction for a fixed sufficiently large \(C\). Starting from zero, its iterates satisfy \(\|c_{j+1}-c_j\|\le2^{-j}\|c_1-c_0\|\), so they are Cauchy and converge in finite-dimensional Euclidean space. Continuity makes the limit \(c(\varepsilon)\) a fixed point. Thus \(F(\varepsilon,c(\varepsilon))=0\), and \(F(\varepsilon,0)=o(\varepsilon)\) gives \(c(\varepsilon)=o(\varepsilon)\). The corrected path has score \(s\). The full-data extensions above lift it into branch \(b\). For a general square-integrable \(s\), truncate and recenter to \(\widetilde s_k\), and set
\[
 s_k=\widetilde s_k-v^{\prime}M^{-1}E_0[R_b^{*}\widetilde s_k].
 \tag{10}
\]
Then \(E_0[R_b^{*}s_k]=0\) and \(s_k\to s\) in \(L^2(P_{0,O})\). Taking the closure specified in \(\mathrm{def{:}branch\text{-}tangents}\) proves
\[
 \mathcal T_b(P_0)=\{s\in\mathcal H_{P_0}:E_0[R_{b,x}s]=0\text{ for all }x\}.
 \tag{11}
\]

It remains to restore the product-rule term omitted by the old formula. Put \(q_x=P_O(G=1,X=x)\). Assumptions \(\mathrm{ass{:}cell\text{-}mass}\) and \(\mathrm{ass{:}group\text{-}overlap}\) imply \(\pi_1=\sum_xq_x>0\). Along an arbitrary observed-data score \(s\), quotient differentiation of \(\nu_x=q_x/\pi_1\) yields
\[
 \dot\nu_x(s)
 =E_0\!\left[\frac{\mathbf 1\{G=1\}}{\pi_1}
 \{\mathbf 1\{X=x\}-\nu_x\}s\right].
 \tag{12}
\]
Since \(\theta_b=\sum_x\nu_xC_b(x)\), equation (12) and \(\mathrm{def{:}normal\text{-}gradients}\) give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \dot\theta_b(s)
 &=\sum_x C_b(x)\dot\nu_x(s)+\sum_x\nu_x\dot C_b(x;s)\\
 &=E_0[\chi_b s]+\sum_xE_0[g^{\circ}_{b,x}s]
 =E_0\!\left[\left\{\chi_b+\sum_xg^{\circ}_{b,x}\right\}s\right].
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{13}
\]
This proves the derivative identity rather than building it into the causal target.

There are finitely many retained normals, so (11) implies \(\mathcal T_b(P_0)^{\perp}=\operatorname{span}\{R_{b,x}:x\in\mathcal X\}\). Combining this with (13) and \(\mathrm{def{:}influence\text{-}classes}\) gives
\[
 \mathcal I_b(P_0)=\chi_b+\sum_xg^{\circ}_{b,x}
 +\operatorname{span}\{R_{b,x}:x\in\mathcal X\}.
 \tag{14}
\]
The conditional-residual normalization gives \(E_0[R_{b,x}\mid G,X]=0\), whereas \(\chi_b\) is measurable with respect to \((G,X)\); hence \(E_0[R_b\chi_b]=0\). Let \(G_b^{\circ}=\sum_xg^{\circ}_{b,x}\), \(\Gamma_b=E_0[R_bR_b^{\prime}]\), and \(u_b=E_0[R_bG_b^{\circ}]\). If \(c\in\ker\Gamma_b\), then \(c^{\prime}R_b=0\) almost surely, so \(c^{\prime}u_b=0\); thus \(u_b\in\operatorname{range}\Gamma_b\). Completing the square yields
\[
 \|\chi_b+G_b^{\circ}+R_b^{\prime}a\|_2^2
 =\|\chi_b+G_b^{\circ}-R_b^{\prime}\Gamma_b^{\dagger}u_b\|_2^2
 +(a+\Gamma_b^{\dagger}u_b)^{\prime}\Gamma_b(a+\Gamma_b^{\dagger}u_b).
 \tag{15}
\]
Minimizing (15) proves the displayed canonical-gradient formula. Moreover \(E_0[\chi_b g^{\circ}_{b,x}]=0\) by the same conditional-residual argument, so its variance is \(E_0[\chi_b^2]\) plus the minimized centered-face variance. This completes every asserted rank, tangent, influence-class, and variance statement.

Write \(E_0=E_{P_{0,O}}\), \(u=J^{-1}\mathbf 1_J\), and \(\mu_{C,t}(x)=(\mu_{2,t}(x),\ldots,\mu_{J+1,t}(x))^{\prime}\). We first identify the causal target. Under conditional parallel trends and no anticipation,
\[
 \delta_1^0(x)=\Delta\mu_g(x),\qquad g=2,\ldots,J+1,
 \tag{1}
\]
so
\[
 E_F[Y_T(1)-Y_T(0)\mid G=1,X=x]
 =\mu_{1,T}(x)-\mu_{1,T-1}(x)-u^{\prime}D(x)
 =C_{\mathrm{PT}}(x).
 \tag{2}
\]
The support assumptions imply \(\pi_1=\sum_xp_X(x)p_1(x)>0\), hence \(\nu_x=p_X(x)p_1(x)/\pi_1\) is well defined. Averaging (2) over \(X\mid G=1\) proves \(\theta(P)=\theta_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_O)\) on \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{PT}}\).

Under the synthetic-mean restriction, the intercept and preperiod equations give \(a(x)=B(x)w(x)\). Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}sc\text{-}rank}\) makes \(B(x)^{\prime}B(x)\) invertible, so \(w(x)\) is uniquely identified by its displayed formula. The final-period equation then gives
\[
 E_F[Y_T(0)\mid G=1,X=x]=w(x)^{\prime}\mu_{C,T}(x),
 \tag{3}
\]
and hence the conditional causal effect is \(C_{\mathrm{SC}}(x)\). Averaging proves \(\theta(P)=\theta_{\mathrm{SC}}(P_O)\) on \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{SC}}\). At \(P_0\in\mathcal M_I\), both equal the same conditional causal effect for every occupied \(x\), so
\[
 C_{\mathrm{PT}}(x)=C_{\mathrm{SC}}(x),
 \qquad \chi_{\mathrm{PT}}=\chi_{\mathrm{SC}}=\chi_0.
 \tag{4}
\]

Define centered stratum faces
\[
 \psi^{\circ}_{\mathrm{PT},x}(a)=g^{\circ}_{\mathrm{PT},x}+R_{\mathrm{PT},x}^{\prime}a,
 \qquad
 \psi^{\circ}_{\mathrm{SC},x}(d)=g^{\circ}_{\mathrm{SC},x}+R_{\mathrm{SC},x}^{\prime}d.
 \tag{5}
\]
By \(\mathrm{lem{:}tangent\text{-}normal\text{-}form}\), adding \(\chi_0\) to sums of these faces exhausts the two influence classes. We now prove that they meet. Suppress \(x\) and the positive factor \(\nu_x\). Adding a PT normal permits every donor weight \(v\) with \(\mathbf 1_J^{\prime}v=1\), producing the conditional-mean differential
\[
 L_{\mathrm{PT}}(v)=\dot\mu_{1,T}-\dot\mu_{1,T-1}
 -v^{\prime}(\dot\mu_{C,T}-\dot\mu_{C,T-1}).
 \tag{6}
\]
For SC, differentiating the full-rank normal equations at \(a=Bw\) gives
\[
 \dot w=(B^{\prime}B)^{-1}B^{\prime}(\dot a-\dot B,w).
 \tag{7}
\]
Consequently the SC affine face consists of
\[
 L_{\mathrm{SC}}(q)=\dot\mu_{1,T}-w^{\prime}\dot\mu_{C,T}
 +q^{\prime}(\dot a-\dot B,w),
 \qquad B^{\prime}q=-\mu_{C,T}.
 \tag{8}
\]
At the intersection, (1) gives \(\mu_{C,T}=\mu_{C,T-1}+\delta_x\mathbf 1_J\). If \(e_0\) selects the intercept row and \(e_-\) selects the period \(T-1\) row, then \(B^{\prime}e_0=\mathbf 1_J\), \(B^{\prime}e_-=\mu_{C,T-1}\), and
\[
 q_*=-e_- -\delta_xe_0
 \quad\text{satisfies}\quad B^{\prime}q_*=-\mu_{C,T}.
 \tag{9}
\]
The intercept rows are fixed, so \(e_0^{\prime}(\dot a-\dot B,w)=0\). Substitution into (8) gives
\[
 L_{\mathrm{SC}}(q_*)
 =\dot\mu_{1,T}-\dot\mu_{1,T-1}
 -w^{\prime}(\dot\mu_{C,T}-\dot\mu_{C,T-1})
 =L_{\mathrm{PT}}(w).
 \tag{10}
\]
Restoring \(\nu_x\), equation (10) supplies equal centered representatives. The product-rule contribution is not hidden: it is the explicitly common term \(\chi_0\) in (4). Thus the full influence classes have nonempty intersection.

By the corrected definitions of \(h_x\) and \(\Omega_x\),
\[
 \psi^{\circ}_{\mathrm{PT},x}(a)-\psi^{\circ}_{\mathrm{SC},x}(d)
 =c(a,d)^{\prime}h_x
 \tag{11}
\]
and positive semidefiniteness gives
\[
 \Omega_x^{1/2}c(a,d)=0
 \Longleftrightarrow
 E_0[\{\psi^{\circ}_{\mathrm{PT},x}(a)-\psi^{\circ}_{\mathrm{SC},x}(d)\}^2\mid X=x]=0.
 \tag{12}
\]
The QP objective is exactly \(E_0[\{\psi^{\circ}_{\mathrm{PT},x}(a)\}^2\mid X=x]\). Feasibility follows from (10). Orthogonal projection onto the finite-dimensional closed affine feasible image gives a unique minimum represented function; the Euclidean minimum-norm convention selects coefficients when rows are redundant. Constant rank and the positive nonzero-eigenvalue margin make the retained coordinate system stable.

Different strata have disjoint support. Moreover the conditional-residual normalization gives
\[
 E_0[\chi_0\psi^{\circ}_{b,x}(a)]
 =E_0\!\left[\chi_0E_0\{\psi^{\circ}_{b,x}(a)\mid G,X\}\right]=0.
 \tag{13}
\]
Therefore the global projection separates into the common composition component and the stratum programs:
\[
 \phi_U=\chi_0+\sum_x\psi^{\circ}_{\mathrm{PT},x}(a_x^U)
 =\chi_0+\sum_x\psi^{\circ}_{\mathrm{SC},x}(d_x^U),
 \tag{14}
\]
and
\[
 V_U(P_0)=E_0[\chi_0^2]+\sum_xp_X(x)\min\mathrm{QP}_x.
 \tag{15}
\]

Finally, an estimator regular on \(\mathcal M_U\) is regular along every quadratic-mean differentiable submodel in either branch, so its regular influence component belongs to both derivative classes. The regular-estimator variance bound in \(\mathrm{lem{:}semiparametric\text{-}convolution\text{-}bound}\), applied to finite collections of branch paths and then to their closed span, gives
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_{P_0}(\text{regular limit})
 \ge \inf_{\phi\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_0)\cap\mathcal I_{\mathrm{SC}}(P_0)}E_0[\phi^2]
 =E_0[\phi_U^2].
 \tag{16}
\]
Equations (14)--(16) give the sharp bound in the local tangent experiment. The cited branchwise laws concern maintained-branch procedures; nothing in this projection proof constructs an attaining estimator, standard error, or multiplier procedure.

Write \(E_0=E_{P_{0,O}}\) and \(\|f\|_0^2=E_0[f^2]\). At the intersection, \(\chi_{\mathrm{PT}}=\chi_{\mathrm{SC}}=\chi_0\). Define
\[
 \psi^{\circ}_{\mathrm{PT},x}(a)=g^{\circ}_{\mathrm{PT},x}+R_{\mathrm{PT},x}^{\prime}a,
 \qquad
 \psi^{\circ}_{\mathrm{SC},x}(d)=g^{\circ}_{\mathrm{SC},x}+R_{\mathrm{SC},x}^{\prime}d.
 \tag{1}
\]
The tangent normal form, disjoint stratum support, and orthogonality of \(\chi_0\) to every conditional-residual piece show that the oracle programs separate by stratum and give
\[
 \phi_{\mathrm{PT}}=\chi_0+\sum_x\psi^{\circ}_{\mathrm{PT},x}(a_x^{\mathrm{or}}),
 \qquad
 \phi_{\mathrm{SC}}=\chi_0+\sum_x\psi^{\circ}_{\mathrm{SC},x}(d_x^{\mathrm{or}}).
 \tag{2}
\]
Thus each branch variance equals \(E_0[\chi_0^2]\) plus its minimized centered-face variance. The common term cancels in the difference. By the definitions of \(h_x\), \(\Omega_x\), and \(c(a,d)\),
\[
 E_0[\{\psi^{\circ}_{\mathrm{PT},x}(a)-\psi^{\circ}_{\mathrm{SC},x}(d)\}^2\mid X=x]
 =c(a,d)^{\prime}\Omega_xc(a,d).
 \tag{3}
\]
Since \(p_X(x)>0\), equations (2)--(3) imply
\[
 \|\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}-\phi_{\mathrm{SC}}\|_0^2
 =\sum_xp_X(x)c(a_x^{\mathrm{or}},d_x^{\mathrm{or}})^{\prime}
 \Omega_xc(a_x^{\mathrm{or}},d_x^{\mathrm{or}}).
 \tag{4}
\]
Every summand is nonnegative. Hence the simultaneous Gram discrepancy vanishes if and only if the two canonical gradients coincide in \(L^2(P_{0,O})\).

Let \(A=\mathcal I_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_0)\), \(B=\mathcal I_{\mathrm{SC}}(P_0)\), and \(C=A\cap B\). These are closed affine sets because their direction spaces are finite normal spans, and \(C\ne\varnothing\) by \(\mathrm{thm{:}union\text{-}envelope}\). If \(L_A\) is the direction space of \(A\), minimality of \(\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\) implies \(\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\perp L_A\). Therefore, for every \(c\in C\subseteq A\),
\[
 \|c\|_0^2=\|\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\|_0^2+\|c-\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\|_0^2.
 \tag{5}
\]
Taking the minimum over \(C\) yields
\[
 V_U=V_{\mathrm{PT}}
 \Longleftrightarrow \phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\in C
 \Longleftrightarrow \phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\in B.
 \tag{6}
\]
Using (1)--(3), the squared distance from \(\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\) to \(B\) is exactly
\[
 \min_{(d_x)}\sum_xp_X(x)c(a_x^{\mathrm{or}},d_x)^{\prime}
 \Omega_xc(a_x^{\mathrm{or}},d_x).
 \tag{7}
\]
This finite-dimensional least-squares minimum is attained; redundant coordinates are handled by a Moore--Penrose inverse. Equations (6)--(7) prove the PT one-sided criterion. Interchanging the branches gives
\[
 V_U=V_{\mathrm{SC}}
 \Longleftrightarrow
 \min_{(a_x)}\sum_xp_X(x)c(a_x,d_x^{\mathrm{or}})^{\prime}
 \Omega_xc(a_x,d_x^{\mathrm{or}})=0.
 \tag{8}
\]

If all three variance bounds coincide, (5) and its SC analogue force \(\phi_U=\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}=\phi_{\mathrm{SC}}\). Conversely, if the branch gradients coincide, their common value belongs to \(C\) and is no larger in norm than any point of either branch class; since \(C\) is contained in each branch class, its minimum has the same norm. Hence \(V_U=V_{\mathrm{PT}}=V_{\mathrm{SC}}\). Together with (4), this proves the simultaneous criterion. Every displayed discrepancy depends only on \(p_X(x)\), \(\Omega_x\), and solutions of finite covariance-weighted quadratic programs, so it is identified from \(P_{0,O}\).

There is one stratum and every group has probability \(1/3\). Thus the support and overlap margins hold because \(p_X=1\) and \(1/3>\epsilon_0\). No anticipation holds by construction. Every untreated final mean change is zero, so conditional parallel trends holds and
\[
 D=(0,0)^{\prime},\qquad \delta_1^0=0,\qquad q_{\mathrm{PT}}(P^{\star})=(0,0)^{\prime}.
 \tag{1}
\]
The augmented donor matrix and target vector are
\[
 B=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\-1&1\\-2&2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad a=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad B^{\prime}B=\begin{pmatrix}6&-4\\-4&6\end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{2}
\]
The eigenvalues are \(2\) and \(10\), so the SC rank margin holds since \(\kappa_0<1\). Solving \(Bw=a\) gives the unique weights \(w=(1/2,1/2)^{\prime}\), which also reproduce the period-three untreated mean. The assumed fourth-moment inequality supplies the remaining model condition. Hence \(P^{\star}\in\mathcal M_I\). Since \(K=1\), each branch contrast equals its own treated average, so
\[
 \chi_{\mathrm{PT}}=\chi_{\mathrm{SC}}=\chi_0=0.
 \tag{3}
\]
Thus the corrected composition term changes none of the following variance calculations.

Define \(z_{g,t}=3\mathbf 1\{G=g\}\varepsilon_{g,t}\). Direct differentiation of a conditional cell mean shows that \(z_{g,t}\) is its mean-zero influence variable. The variables are pairwise orthogonal, with variances by time within group
\[
 (3,3,3),\qquad (3,3/2,3/2),\qquad (6,6,6).
 \tag{4}
\]
The PT face, parameterized by the donor-two weight \(v\), is
\[
 \psi_{\mathrm{PT}}(v)=(z_{1,3}-z_{1,2})
 -v(z_{2,3}-z_{2,2})-(1-v)(z_{3,3}-z_{3,2}).
 \tag{5}
\]
Consequently
\[
 \|\psi_{\mathrm{PT}}(v)\|_0^2=6+3v^2+12(1-v)^2.
 \tag{6}
\]
The derivative is \(30v-24\), so the unique minimizer is \(v=4/5\), and
\[
 V_{\mathrm{PT}}(P^{\star})=6+3(4/5)^2+12(1/5)^2=\frac{42}{5}.
 \tag{7}
\]
For \(J=2\), the donor-change contrast has positive variance \(15\); hence the PT normal Gram has rank one.

For SC, \(u=(0,-2,1)^{\prime}\) spans \(\ker(B^{\prime})\). Differentiating the full-rank normal equations yields
\[
 \dot w=(B^{\prime}B)^{-1}B^{\prime}(\dot a-\dot B,w).
 \tag{8}
\]
The unrestricted SC cell-mean coefficients, ordered by time within groups one, two, and three, are
\[
 (-2/5,-4/5,1),\qquad (1/5,2/5,-1/2),\qquad (1/5,2/5,-1/2).
 \tag{9}
\]
Adding \(\beta u^{\prime}(\dot a-\dot B,w)\) changes only preperiod coefficients. Using (4), their variance contribution is
\[
 Q(\beta)=\frac{207}{8}\beta^2+\frac35\beta+\frac{99}{25}.
 \tag{10}
\]
It is uniquely minimized at \(\beta^{\mathrm{or}}=-4/345\), with minimum \(91/23\). The final-period contribution is \(39/8\), and therefore
\[
 V_{\mathrm{SC}}(P^{\star})=\frac{39}{8}+\frac{91}{23}=\frac{1625}{184}.
 \tag{11}
\]

SC normals have only preperiod coordinates, so equality with the PT face forces \(v=1/2\) from the final donor coefficients. Equality of the preperiod coefficients then forces \(\beta=-1/5\), giving the unique common representative with coefficients
\[
 (0,-1,1),\qquad (0,1/2,-1/2),\qquad (0,1/2,-1/2).
 \tag{12}
\]
Its variance is
\[
 V_U(P^{\star})=6+3(1/2)^2+12(1/2)^2=\frac{39}{4}.
 \tag{13}
\]
The PT oracle has \(v=4/5\ne1/2\), and the SC oracle has \(\beta=-4/345\ne-1/5\). The one-sided criteria in \(\mathrm{thm{:}oracle\text{-}adaptation\text{-}frontier}\) therefore make both discrepancies strictly positive. Subtraction gives
\[
 V_U-V_{\mathrm{PT}}=\frac{27}{20},
 \qquad V_U-V_{\mathrm{SC}}=\frac{169}{184}.
 \tag{14}
\]
All finite-support Gram entries, unique quadratic minimizers, and minimized values vary continuously with cell probabilities, means, and second moments while the nonzero spectral margins persist. At \(P^{\star}\), full rank, positive unequal change variances, unequal oracle weights, and both strict gaps hold. Hence they persist on a relatively open intersection neighborhood satisfying the fourth-moment envelope. This proves the final stability assertion without moving any weight or moment boundary.

If \(J=1\), then \(\mathbf 1_J\mathbf 1_J^{\prime}=1\), and \(\mathrm{def{:}restriction\text{-}maps}\) gives
\[
 A_{\mathrm{PT}}=I_1-1=0,
 \qquad r_{\mathrm{PT},x}=0.
 \tag{1}
\]
The corrected tangent normal form therefore gives
\[
 \mathcal T_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_0)=\mathcal H_{P_0},
 \qquad \mathcal I_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_0)=\{\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}\},
 \tag{2}
\]
where \(\phi_{\mathrm{PT}}=\chi_{\mathrm{PT}}+\sum_xg^{\circ}_{\mathrm{PT},x}\); the composition term is included explicitly.

With one donor the intercept restriction forces \(w_2(x)=1\), and the SC restriction gives \(\mu_{1,t}(x)=\mu_{2,t}(x)\) for \(t<T\). Hence, throughout the SC branch,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \theta_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_O)
 &=\sum_x\nu_x\{\mu_{1,T}-\mu_{1,T-1}-\mu_{2,T}+\mu_{2,T-1}\}\\
 &=\sum_x\nu_x\{\mu_{1,T}-\mu_{2,T}\}
 =\theta_{\mathrm{SC}}(P_O).
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{3}
\]
Thus their derivatives agree on every SC tangent. Since the singleton PT influence function represents the PT derivative on all of \(\mathcal H_{P_0}\), it belongs to \(\mathcal I_{\mathrm{SC}}(P_0)\). Therefore
\[
 \mathcal I_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_0)\subseteq\mathcal I_{\mathrm{SC}}(P_0),
 \qquad \phi_U=\phi_{\mathrm{PT}},
 \qquad V_U=V_{\mathrm{PT}}.
 \tag{4}
\]

For \(T=2\), put \(\Delta Y=Y_2-Y_1\) and \(m_g(x)=E_O[\Delta Y\mid G=g,X=x]\). Overlap gives positive denominators. Direct quotient and conditional-mean differentiation gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \phi_{\mathrm{PT}}(O)
 &=\frac{\mathbf 1\{G=1\}}{\pi_1}\{\Delta Y-m_1(X)\}
 -\frac{\mathbf 1\{G=2\}}{\pi_1}\frac{p_1(X)}{p_2(X)}\{\Delta Y-m_2(X)\}\\
 &\quad+\frac{\mathbf 1\{G=1\}}{\pi_1}\{m_1(X)-m_2(X)-\theta\}.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{5}
\]
The first two terms are conditional-residual pieces; the last is exactly the treated-composition gradient. Equation (5) is mean zero and its covariance with every score equals the derivative of the panel ATT functional. Under the group relabeling, it is the panel efficient influence function reported in SantAnnaZhao2020, Proposition 1(a), equations (2.11)--(2.12), as recorded in the corrected cited leaf.

Put \(\Pi_x=B(x)\{B(x)^{\prime}B(x)\}^{-1}B(x)^{\prime}\). Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}sc\text{-}rank}\) makes this the orthogonal projector onto the \(J\)-dimensional column space of \(B(x)\), so \(I_T-\Pi_x\) has rank \(T-J\). At an SC law, \(a(x)=B(x)w(x)\). Differentiating \(\Pi_xB(x)=B(x)\) yields
\[
 \dot\Pi_xB(x)w(x)=(I_T-\Pi_x)\dot B(x)w(x).
 \tag{1}
\]
Since \(r_{\mathrm{SC},x}=(I_T-\Pi_x)a(x)\),
\[
 \dot r_{\mathrm{SC},x}=(I_T-\Pi_x)\{\dot a(x)-\dot B(x)w(x)\}.
 \tag{2}
\]
The corrected definition of \(R_{\mathrm{SC},x}\) uses the conditional-residual Riesz version of precisely this derivative; conditional centering does not alter the deterministic range in (2). Thus the covariance range of \(R_{\mathrm{SC},x}\) is contained in \(\operatorname{range}(I_T-\Pi_x)\), proving the rank bound \(T-J\). If the residualized covariance form is positive definite on that range, its covariance rank equals the range dimension, giving equality.

Fix \(x\). When \(J=T\), \(B(x)\) is square. Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}sc\text{-}rank}\) gives \(\lambda_{\min}\{B(x)^{\prime}B(x)\}\ge\kappa_0>0\), so \(B(x)\) is invertible and
\[
 B(x)\{B(x)^{\prime}B(x)\}^{-1}B(x)^{\prime}=I_T.
 \tag{1}
\]
Therefore \(r_{\mathrm{SC},x}=0\) throughout the full-rank neighborhood, and its derivative and normalized Riesz vector are zero. Equivalently, \(\mathrm{lem{:}sc\text{-}profiled\text{-}normal\text{-}rank}\) gives rank at most \(T-J=0\).

The corrected tangent normal form now gives
\[
 \mathcal T_{\mathrm{SC}}(P_0)=\mathcal H_{P_0},
 \qquad
 \mathcal I_{\mathrm{SC}}(P_0)
 =\left\{\chi_{\mathrm{SC}}+\sum_xg^{\circ}_{\mathrm{SC},x}\right\}
 =\{\phi_{\mathrm{SC}}\}.
 \tag{2}
\]
The common composition term is present in the singleton. The union-envelope theorem proves that the intersection with \(\mathcal I_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_0)\) is nonempty. Since (2) is a singleton,
\[
 \mathcal I_{\mathrm{PT}}(P_0)\cap\mathcal I_{\mathrm{SC}}(P_0)=\{\phi_{\mathrm{SC}}\}.
 \tag{3}
\]
The definitions of the union gradient and variances therefore give \(\phi_U=\phi_{\mathrm{SC}}\) and \(V_U=V_{\mathrm{SC}}\).

Choose the fixed margins so that \(P^{\star}\) satisfies them with slack. For sufficiently small fixed \(\delta\ne0\), retain both donor mean paths and all innovation laws, but replace the treated untreated mean path by
\[
 (1/2+\delta)(-1,-2,-2)+(1/2-\delta)(1,2,2)=(-2\delta,-4\delta,-4\delta).
 \tag{1}
\]
Give the treated group the same additive final treatment effect and call the law \(Q_\delta\). Every untreated final mean change remains zero, so PT holds. The donor matrix is unchanged, and the treated path is reproduced by the unique weights
\[
 w_\delta=(1/2+\delta,1/2-\delta)^{\prime},
 \tag{2}
\]
so SC also holds. Continuity preserves the strict support, moment, rank, spectral-gap, and variance margins for small \(|\delta|\). Thus \(Q_\delta\in\mathcal M_I\).

There is one covariate stratum. On either branch \(C_b(X)=\theta_b\) is constant, and hence the corrected composition terms satisfy
\[
 \chi_{\mathrm{PT}}(Q_\delta)=\chi_{\mathrm{SC}}(Q_\delta)=0.
 \tag{3}
\]
Accordingly the chart difference is exactly the centered chart difference used below; adding the required branch-specific \(\chi_b(P)\) to \(\mathrm{def{:}local\text{-}score\text{-}extension}\) does not alter the witness calculation.

Fix an integer \(m\). Construct two sequences that equal \(Q_\delta\) at coordinate \(m\) and \(P^{\star}\) elsewhere, labeling coordinate \(m\) by PT in the first and by SC in the second. Each belongs to \(\mathfrak L_U(P^{\star})\): after the exceptional coordinate it is identically \(P^{\star}\), so its QMD score and remainder are eventually zero, and each coordinate obeys the fixed margins. Thus the frozen sequence class contains, at every sample size, two admissibly labeled copies of the same observed law.

Let \(z_{g,t}=3\mathbf 1\{G=g\}\{Y_t-\mu_{g,t}\}\). At \(Q_\delta\),
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(z_{2,3})=\frac32,
 \qquad \operatorname{Var}(z_{3,3})=6.
 \tag{4}
\]
At \(P^{\star}\), the common score has final donor coefficients \((-1/2,-1/2)\). The PT extension freezes its center normal coefficient, and donor laws are unchanged, so those coefficients remain \((-1/2,-1/2)\) at \(Q_\delta\). The SC normal uses only preperiod coordinates, whereas (2) makes the SC final donor coefficients \((-1/2-\delta,-1/2+\delta)\). Hence, for
\[
 \Delta_\delta=\phi_U^{\mathrm{loc}}(Q_\delta;\mathrm{PT},P^{\star})
 -\phi_U^{\mathrm{loc}}(Q_\delta;\mathrm{SC},P^{\star}),
 \tag{5}
\]
the final-innovation component is \(\delta(z_{2,3}-z_{3,3})\). Every remaining component uses other group-period innovations and is orthogonal to it. Therefore
\[
 E_{Q_\delta}[\Delta_\delta^2]
 \ge\delta^2\left(\frac32+6\right)=\frac{15}{2}\delta^2>0.
 \tag{6}
\]
Both chart scores are mean zero, so \(E_{Q_\delta}[\Delta_\delta]=0\).

If one estimator had both chart expansions uniformly over the frozen class, coupling the two sequences at sample size \(m\) through the same iid sample from \(Q_\delta\) and subtracting the expansions would give
\[
 S_m=m^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^m\Delta_\delta(O_i)=o_{Q_\delta}(1).
 \tag{7}
\]
But iid sampling and (6) imply \(E[S_m^2]=E[\Delta_\delta^2]\ge15\delta^2/2\). Because \(\Delta_\delta\) is a bounded linear combination of finitely many Rademacher innovations,
\[
 E[S_m^4]=m^{-1}E[\Delta_\delta^4]+3(1-m^{-1})E[\Delta_\delta^2]^2
 \tag{8}
\]
is uniformly bounded. Hence \((S_m^2)\) is uniformly integrable. Convergence in probability in (7) would then imply \(E[S_m^2]\to0\), contradicting (6).

Thus no estimator has both chart expansions uniformly over \(\mathfrak L_U(P^{\star})\). Since asymptotic linearity is a necessary conjunct of the requested one-step, variance, and multiplier result, the full affirmative result is false. The argument leaves open only a different theorem on a redesigned common neighborhood with common score and remainder bounds and without arbitrary finite-coordinate splicing.
